activities.caption: file each outcome under its predicting trait
activities.name: perbTraitBuckets

config.prompt: File each real-world outcome under the trait that predicts it:

items.label: health outcomes, partly through chronic stress load
anxiety and vulnerability to negative emotion
mortality risk in longitudinal cohorts (low conscientiousness plus high neuroticism)

config.why: The Terman study follow-ups are the classic evidence. Traits are durable defaults, not fate — and the five are dimensions, not types.

config.prompt: Big Five rank-order correlations across 40-plus years — place the marker at the stability figure:
config.why: About 0.7, rising with age — and yet traits drift: conscientiousness and agreeableness rise, neuroticism falls through adulthood (Roberts and colleagues' 2007 meta-analysis — the maturity principle).

statements.s: A high heritability estimate means the trait is fixed in the individual.
statements.why: Heritability describes variation within a population at a time, not the changeability of an individual.

statements.s: Height is 80-90% heritable and rose centimetre by centimetre as nutrition improved.
statements.why: Both true at once — the standard demonstration that heritability is not fate.

statements.s: Heritability estimates for personality in twin studies are consistent across cultures.
statements.why: About 40-60% for personality, consistent across cultures.

statements.s: A trait can be strongly heritable and still shift across generations.
statements.why: The height example again — heritability within a population constrains nothing about change across environments.

activities.anchor: you are an extravert or an introvert
activities.caption: drag the divider — slider or box
activities.name: perbDimCompare

config.prompt: Dimensions versus types — drag the divider.

before.label: a dimension
before.text: One continuous slider: most people sit near the middle, and scores differ in degree.

after.label: a type
after.text: A box manufactured by cutting the slider at an arbitrary midpoint — near-identical scores land on opposite sides.

config.why: The Big Five measures dimensions — everyone sits somewhere on each of the five sliders. Type language has to be manufactured by that cut, exactly the move the MBTI makes.

activities.anchor: Freud's model made personality a dynamic compromise
activities.caption: pair each concept with its role
activities.name: perbFreudMatch

config.prompt: What survived from the older schools — pair each concept with its role:

pairs.right: the manager deploying defence mechanisms — repression, projection, rationalisation — when conflict generates anxiety
the motivational ladder from physiological needs through safety, belonging and esteem to self-actualisation
empathy, genuineness, unconditional positive regard — previewing therapy's common factors

config.why: As testable theory both schools fared poorly — projective instruments show weak reliability and validity — but as vocabularies for lived experience they remain unrivalled.

activities.anchor: relocated personality from inside the person to a loop
activities.caption: find the faulty line — a social-cognitive briefing
activities.name: perbEfficacySpot

config.prompt: One line of this social-cognitive briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: Reciprocal determinism: thoughts, behaviour and environment each shape the others.
Self-efficacy — beliefs about one's own capability — predicts persistence, choice of challenges and coping better than skill alone does.
Self-efficacy is fixed by skill level and cannot be trained.
The framework's weakness: heavy on mechanisms, light on a compact, cross-culturally validated inventory.
config.correction: Self-efficacy is itself trainable, chiefly through mastery experiences.
config.why: The honest synthesis: the Big Five describes the landscape; social-cognitive theory explains some of the terrain-forming processes.

config.q: In the digital-footprint studies, what did models trained on social-media 'likes' achieve?
choices: Accuracy comparable to a work colleague's rating
Accuracy comparable to a spouse's rating
config.why: Predicting self-reported Big Five scores with accuracy comparable to a spouse's rating — impressive, and a privacy problem, not a new theory of personality.

events.title: The lexical catalogue
events.text: Allport and Odbert comb 18,000 trait terms — the dictionary as a pre-computed catalogue of human differences.

events.title: Mischel's challenge
events.text: Single behaviours correlate with trait ratings at only about 0.3 — traits briefly declared illusory.

events.title: The if-then settlement
events.text: Mischel and Shoda: stable if-then signatures — traits predict behaviour aggregated over situations.

events.title: The maturity principle
events.text: Roberts and colleagues' meta-analysis: conscientiousness and agreeableness rise, neuroticism falls through adulthood.

events.title: The Tsimané edge case
events.text: Among the Bolivian forager-horticulturalists the Big Five structure comes apart — the universality claim gains a boundary.
